content: 1. In Moldova, efforts have been made to improve and disseminate standardized operating procedures for the collection, entry, and validation of administrative data on violence against women (VAW). This aligns with global technical guidance aimed at enhancing the collection and use of such data. 2. It is essential to establish and publicly share standards for the periodicity, transparency, and availability of VAW administrative data. Data compilation and reporting should follow a set schedule and adhere to the United Nations Fundamental Principles of Official Statistics. 3. At a minimum, official reports analyzing VAW administrative data should be made publicly available on an annual basis. 4. Anonymized data must be accessible to relevant government stakeholders, including service providers, managers, legislators, policymakers, gender specialists, and others responsible for VAW response. It should also be available to the general public, media, civil society organizations (CSOs), development partners, and researchers. 5. Data availability is critical for ensuring accountability among duty-bearers. The origin of the data (metadata) must be clearly stated. 6. Some VAW administrative data portals only publish reports, but all shared data should be anonymized and aggregated to maintain confidentiality. This includes suppressing small number counts that could lead to the identification of respondents and limiting access to potentially identifying variables, such as geographic or location-based data. 7. Only aggregated data (macodata) should be made publicly available. Macodata refers to grouped individual-level records (microdata), which are only accessible under strict oversight to qualified researchers or government data analysts who have undergone ethics training and signed confidentiality agreements. 8. In Spain, the Organic Law on Comprehensive Protection Measures against Gender-Based Violence, passed in 2004, established the Government Delegation against Gender-Based Violence. This delegation includes a Sub-directorate General for Awareness, Prevention, and Studies of Gender-Based Violence, which coordinates multisectoral efforts to improve VAW prevention and response using administrative data. 9. The Sub-directorate General acts as the national coordination mechanism for VAW administrative data. It provides secretariat functions for the State Observatory on Violence, an inter-ministerial body with representatives from health, education, justice, police, social services, academia, and CSOs. 10. The State Observatory standardizes VAW administrative data, prepares studies and reports, and proposes actions to prevent and respond to VAW. It collects, analyzes, and reports data from specialized VAW services, such as shelters, hotlines, and economic support programs. 11. Spain’s Gender Violence Portal implements best practices for periodicity, transparency, data availability, and confidentiality. It publishes an annual calendar of data releases and an inventory of statistical operations with metadata for each variable, developed in collaboration with the National Statistics Office (NSO). 12. The portal provides regularly updated statistics, monthly and annual reports, and recommendations from the State Observatory on Violence. All data are anonymized, and statistics are produced following written standards that ensure confidentiality and data protection, in alignment with national statistics laws. 13. The portal includes features such as data visualizations, summary tables, and short stories to communicate key figures and trends to various audiences, including the general public, media, policymakers, and researchers. 14. In Mexico, the General Law on Women’s Access to a Life Free of Violence, enacted in 2007, mandated the creation of a National Data and Information Bank on Violence Against Women to evaluate the effectiveness of measures to prevent, address, and eradicate violence. 15. Mexico’s federal structure includes 32 states, each of which has passed or amended VAW laws to establish state-level VAW data banks. Many states use the information technology infrastructure provided by the National Data Bank. 16. Zacatecas’ BANEVIM (Banco Estatal de Datos sobre Violencia contra las Mujeres) is an example of a state-level VAW data portal. It is updated monthly and includes 12 standard indicators, such as types of VAW, survivor and perpetrator demographics, and details about the incidents. 17. BANEVIM publishes quarterly and semi-annual reports and infographics. It also conducts spatial analyses to identify geographic hotspots and analyzes survivors’ reported needs and barriers to accessing services. 18. One analysis identified transportation as a barrier for survivors seeking support services and pursuing legal cases. In response, the Women’s Justice Centre of the Attorney General’s Office implemented a state-wide program to provide pre-paid public transportation tickets to help survivors access specialized VAW services and legal support. 19. Effective data communication requires dialogue between data producers and users before and after data production. This helps ensure that data products meet the needs of various audiences and improve VAW prevention and response efforts. 20. Improving data literacy among media, legislators, and other stakeholders is essential for advancing the use of VAW administrative data. This includes understanding that increased reporting of VAW cases may reflect improved service delivery and data recording rather than an actual rise in cases. 21. Data communication products should include both quantitative information (e.g., numbers and trends) and qualitative information (e.g., anonymized survivor stories) to effectively convey the human impact of VAW and foster support for related policies and programs. 22. Administrative data should be contextualized and triangulated with other data sources, such as academic research and qualitative inquiries, to provide a comprehensive understanding of VAW and inform policy options. 23. Data-driven dialogue, incorporating both quantitative and qualitative data, is a promising practice for advancing government responses to VAW. It is important to remind data users that behind the numbers are stories of human suffering and resilience. Survivor stories, shared with consent and anonymity, can serve as powerful messages to raise awareness and drive action.
